opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few things that really have to be there, and some of them are not what people usually emphasize.

First, the system has to build an internal representation of the world, not just of text describing it. Language is a very compressed, very human-filtered view of reality. It's powerful, but much of what matters physically, like spatial structure, how objects persist, how things move and interact, is barely written down. So a world model needs to learn from rich sensory input, especially vision, and form representations that capture that structure. For me, representation learning is still the core. If the representation is weak, everything on top of it is fragile.

Second, it has to be predictive in a meaningful sense. It isn't enough to recognize what's in front of you. You need to anticipate what happens next, and especially what happens if *you* do something. That means the model has to be action-conditioned. A world model that can't reason about the consequences of interventions is closer to a very good video generator than to a model of the world. Generating pixels that look plausible is a different goal from understanding dynamics, and I think the field sometimes conflates the two.

Third, it should predict at the right level of abstraction. Humans don't simulate every pixel or every leaf moving in the wind. We predict the things that matter for what we're trying to do. So I believe the prediction should mostly happen in a learned latent space, keeping what's relevant and discarding what's unpredictable or unimportant.

Fourth, there has to be some kind of memory and persistence. The world doesn't reset every few seconds. Objects you saw a minute ago still exist when they're out of view. A system that lacks a consistent, persistent state, spatially and over time, will keep contradicting itself.

And finally, it should be usable for planning and decision-making. Ultimately, the reason to have a world model is so an agent can imagine, compare options, and act well in the real world. If it can't close that loop, from perception to prediction to action, then I'm not sure we've really built a world model yet. We may have built something impressive, but not the thing that lets intelligence be grounded in reality.

So, put simply: grounded representations, action-conditioned prediction, the right abstraction, persistent memory, and a connection to planning. Today, we have pieces of each, but we're still quite far from putting them together in one system.

r001.rationale: The response makes building a grounded representation of the physical world the system’s core task, emphasizing physical structure, persistence, and dynamics.

r002.rationale: It calls memory and persistence necessary, but does not identify memory as an intermediate component in the system.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about what a world model actually needs, I keep coming back to a few things that, frankly, most of today's systems only partially have.

The first is a real sense of space and time. Not just recognizing what's in an image, but understanding that objects persist, that they occupy a location, and that when the camera moves or the agent moves, the scene changes in a consistent, predictable way. A lot of current video models look impressive for a few seconds and then things drift, objects pop in and out, geometry doesn't stay stable. That's a sign the model hasn't really internalized the structure of the physical world. It's pattern-matching on pixels rather than reasoning about a scene.

The second is memory. A world model has to remember what it has seen. If you walk through a room, turn around, and walk back, the room should still be there with the same layout. Humans do this effortlessly. Most generative models today have very short effective context, so they essentially forget the world they just created. Without persistent memory, you can't do long-horizon tasks, and you can't build an agent that actually operates in an environment over time.

The third is that it has to support action. A world model isn't just a passive video generator. The whole point is that you can ask "what happens if I do this," and get a plausible answer. That means the representation has to be conditioned on actions, and it has to be useful for planning and decision making, not only for producing something that looks nice to a human viewer. This is where I think the distinction between "video generation" and "world modeling" really matters. They share a lot of machinery, but the goals are different.

And then underneath all of this, I'd argue the representation matters a great deal. There's been a tendency to think you can throw enough data and compute at a pixel-space diffusion model and everything else emerges. I'm somewhat skeptical of that. We've found that having a strong visual representation, something closer to how self-supervised encoders see the world, makes the downstream model learn faster and behave more coherently. The model should understand the world in a semantic, structured space, and pixels should be more of an output format than the thing it reasons in.

So if I had to summarize: spatial and temporal consistency, long-term memory, action-conditioned prediction, and a good underlying representation. If you get those four, you have something that starts to deserve the name "world model." If you're missing one of them, you have a very good demo but probably not a system you can build a real agent on top of.

r001.rationale: The response presents spatial and temporal understanding of the physical world as its first requirement, emphasizing persistent objects, stable geometry, and predictable scene changes.

r002.rationale: It explicitly names memory as the second requirement and says a world model has to remember what it has seen to support long-horizon tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think the essential thing is that the model needs to understand how the world changes, especially in response to actions. It’s not enough to recognize what’s in an image or generate a plausible video. If I take an action, what happens next? And if I take a different action, how does the outcome change?

That requires a representation of the world that captures the things that matter for the task, some memory of what the system has observed, and a way to predict future states. It also needs to handle uncertainty, because you never observe everything and you can’t predict everything perfectly.

Then you need to connect that prediction to decision-making. Can the system use its model to compare possible actions, choose one, and update its understanding when the actual outcome differs from its prediction? To me, that loop—observation, prediction, action, and feedback—is what makes a world model useful as part of a system.

r001.rationale: The response calls understanding how the world changes the essential thing and emphasizes action-conditioned outcomes, which conveys understanding the physical world as the system’s foremost task.

r002.rationale: It explicitly includes memory of what the system has observed among the requirements for a world model, identifying memory as a necessary component.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the essential thing is that the model captures how the world changes, including how it changes in response to our actions. Given what I’ve observed and an action I might take, can it predict what happens next? And can I use that prediction to make a better decision?

That requires more than generating a plausible-looking video. The model needs to preserve the aspects of the world that matter for the task—objects, their relationships, motion, and physical constraints. It also needs some memory, because a single observation doesn’t tell you the full state of the world. If something moves out of view, it shouldn’t simply cease to exist in the model.

And uncertainty matters. There may be several possible outcomes, so the system shouldn’t always commit to one future with complete confidence. Ultimately, I would judge a world model by whether its predictions help an agent plan, act, and learn from what actually happens. Visual realism can be useful, but that ability to support action is the more fundamental requirement.

r001.rationale: The response makes modeling how the world changes, responds to actions, and obeys physical constraints the essential requirement, and says support for action is more fundamental than visual realism.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says the model needs memory to represent state beyond a single observation, including objects that move out of view.
